abstract.p: Juvenile colorectal polyps (JCP) are frequent in children and are associated with type 2 inflammation and local IgE synthesis. Our previous work showed that children with JCP in our cohort are sensitized to food allergens. Here, we characterized the bacterial microbiota in fecal samples from food-sensitized children with JCP (FSS) and healthy controls (CS), as well as in JCP tissues and surrounding control tissues (SCT), using 16S rRNA gene sequencing. Although sample richness was comparable across groups, community composition clearly separated fecal from tissue samples and distinguished FSS from CS. ANCOM-BC analysis revealed a distinct microbial profile in FSS, with significant enrichment of genera including Prevotella and Sutterella, and a corresponding reduction in Akkermansia, Veillonella, and several butyrate-producing taxa relative to the CS group. JCP were characterized by enrichment of genera previously associated with inflammatory conditions, including Escherichia, Fusobacterium, and Streptococcus, compared to CS and FSS samples. Notably Akkermansia—depleted in FSS compared to CS—was enriched in JCP when contrasted with FSS, highlighting differences between tissue and fecal microbial profiles across independent cohorts. When compared to the SCT group, JCP samples exhibited higher abundances of Blautia, Phocaeicola, and Dorea. These findings suggest that JCP are associated with a distinct microbial profile across multiple comparisons, whereas FSS is primarily defined by a relative depletion of taxa commonly linked to gut homeostasis. This study provides, to our knowledge, the first comprehensive characterization of the JCP-associated microbiota in food-sensitized pediatric patients, suggesting a potential link between microbial composition and allergic-type inflammation within the polyp microenvironment. Given the limited sample size, particularly for the SCT group, these findings should be considered exploratory.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Food allergy is one of the most prevalent allergic conditions after asthma and rhinitis, with an increasing incidence in the last decades of around 2–7% worldwide1. The pattern and prevalence of food allergy vary among regions and populations. Allergies have been classified as IgE or non-IgE-mediated conditions, in which IgE causes an abnormal immune response to diverse allergens, with a wide spectrum of clinical symptoms from mild to life-threatening, varying among affected individuals. Proteins from cow’s milk, peanuts, and soy are the major food allergens for pediatric population. Several studies have demonstrated that differences in prevalence and incidence of allergic diseases are due to differences in lifestyle worldwide, suggesting that environmental factors are associated with allergies, including food sensitivity1,2.

IgE sensitization represents a key indicator in the trajectory leading to atopic and allergic disorders, such as atopic dermatitis, food allergy, allergic rhinitis, and asthma. Nevertheless, the presence of sensitization alone does not inevitably translate into clinical disease3. Longitudinal birth cohort studies indicate that IgE sensitization increases throughout childhood4,5. While a proportion of sensitized children remain asymptomatic, IgE sensitization is linked to a higher likelihood of developing allergic conditions, a risk that is further amplified in cases of sensitization to multiple allergens (polysensitization)6.

Evidence in experimental animals strongly suggests that the microbiota is not just beneficial, but necessary for the establishment of oral tolerance. Germ-free mice show a reduction in the gut-associated lymphoid tissues, and they mount a type 2 (Th2) inflammatory response after oral sensitization with ovalbumin, compatible with the lack of oral tolerance7. Also, when mice treated with a cocktail of broad-spectrum antibiotics are sensitized to peanuts, they induce an allergic response with high IgE levels and circulating basophils8,9. These studies unequivocally demonstrate that the microbiota has a relevant role in gut mucosa immune system development and regulation.

The involvement of commensal bacteria in regulatory T cell (Treg) responses has been described. Clostridia, which play a role in the generation of short-chain fatty acids by fermentation of dietary fiber, are known to enhance differentiation of peripheral Treg cells. At the same time, butyrate was demonstrated to epigenetically regulate Foxp3 expression10. Elegant studies in mice by Stefka et al.11 showed that mucosa-associated Firmicutes belonging to the class Clostridia are the taxa responsible for protecting against peanut sensitization.

While most of the evidence arises from experimental mice models, several reports on pediatric cohorts have also shown that microbiota composition differs among healthy and allergic children10. For instance, fecal microbiota from healthy children shows a dominance of Lactobacillales, Bifidobacteriales, and Enterobacteriales12. Children with cow’s milk protein allergy show higher levels of anaerobic bacteria, and lower abundance of Bacteroidetes, compared to healthy children whereas the levels of Firmicutes, Clostridia, and Bacteroidales vary among studies13. A recent report on the fecal microbiota of IgE food-sensitized children found increased abundances of Firmicutes and decreased abundances of the Bacteroidetes phylum, while differences were observed depending on the allergen14.

Juvenile colorectal polyps are the most common gut polyp type in children15. Polyps are normally resected, while patients with unique polyps sometimes suffer recurrence, patients with juvenile polyposis are followed up due the potential risk of developing colorectal cancer. We have previously characterized colorectal polyps in a cohort of children sensitized to food allergens16–18. Polyps were of inflammatory type and no adenomatous regions were histologically observed. These patients showed increased serum and tissue IgE levels with high levels of food-specific IgE. In addition, we found that polyps present a type 2 environment and are rich in eosinophils with elevated levels of IL-4, IL-5, and IL-13 but not IFN-γ16,18. We have retrieved cow’s milk protein-specific Th2 cells from peripheral blood and from the polyps of these patients and demonstrated that germinal centers within the polyps are a site of active IgE synthesis16,17. Our results suggest that polyps are of allergic origin, however, the gut microbiota from these patients has not been explored so far.

Given the established role of gut microbiota in shaping mucosal immune responses, particularly in regulating the balance between regulatory T cells and type 2 inflammation, alterations in microbial communities could contribute to the Th2-skewed environment previously described in our cohort. However, the microbiota composition of food-sensitized children with juvenile colorectal polyps has not been investigated so far.
Therefore, we hypothesized that children with food sensitization and JCP would exhibit a distinct gut microbial signature associated with their previously described type 2 immune phenotype.

sec.title: Analysis of the microbial composition of feces from healthy and food-sensitized children and polyp tissue
sec.p: We characterized the bacterial microbiota of feces from patients sensitized to food allergens with polyps and from healthy children. Tissue-associated bacteria of juvenile colorectal polyps (JCP) and surrounding control tissue (SCT) were also analyzed.

Differences in within-sample bacterial diversity among groups were assessed using α-diversity metrics, including Faith’s phylogenetic diversity (PD) and Shannon entropy and Fig. 1 shows a box-and-whisker box plot for α-diversity based on 16S rRNA gene features across the four groups: fecal samples from food-sensitized children with JCP (FSS), control samples (CS), JCP and SCT samples. No significant differences among these categories were observed in both α-diversity analyses.Fig. 1
Box and whisker plot for α-diversity based on 16S rRNA gene features. (A) The vertical axis displays the Faith phylogenetic diversity index (Faith PD) for the four categories analyzed: FSS, CS, JCP and SCT. (B) The vertical axis displays the Shannon diversity index (SDI) for the same categories above. The number of samples used in this analysis for each group was denoted by n.

Differences in between-sample bacterial community composition among groups were assessed using β-diversity metrics, specifically weighted and unweighted UniFrac distances, which account for the relative abundance of taxa and the presence or absence of taxa, respectively19. This analysis reveals distance-based analysis of microbial community dissimilarity across sample types and sensitization groups. Figure 2 shows box-and-whisker plot of the distance between samples from the four different categories (SCT, JCP, FSS and CS) for unweighted UniFrac (panel A) and weighted UniFrac (panel B) distances. Pairwise PERMANOVA analyses revealed significant differences among SCT, JCP, FSS, and CS samples, except for tissue samples JCP and SCT, which did not differ significantly (Supplementary Table 1).Fig. 2
Box and whisker plot for β -diversity based on 16S rRNA gene features. The vertical axis displays the distance among the samples from different categories: FSS (n = 11), CS (n = 19), JCP (n = 14) and SCT (n = 5). The top panel corresponds to the unweighted UniFrac distance while the bottom panel corresponds to the weighted UniFrac distance. Significance was assessed using PERMANOVA (*p-value < 0.002). Grey dots indicate outliers. Within-group distances were added in the plot as a reference.

To further explore patterns of sample similarity and dissimilarity, β-diversity was visualized using principal coordinate analysis (PCoA). Figure 3A depicts the first two axes of the PCoA based on unweighted UniFrac distances, with axes A1 and A2 separating tissue and stool samples. Additionally, axes A1 and A4 separate FSS (orange dots) and CS (blue dots) samples (Fig. 3B). PCoA plots based on weighted UniFrac distance are shown in Supplementary Figure 1, with variance mainly concentrated on the first two axes, while axes A1 and A4 separate feces samples.Fig. 3
Principal coordinate analysis (PCoA) based on unweighted UniFrac distances illustrating differences in microbiota composition from tissue and stool samples. Each dot corresponds to one sample. (A) The first two axes (A1 and A2) distinguish tissue samples from stool samples, indicating clear differences in their microbial communities across independently sampled cohorts. (B) When considering A1 and A4, stool samples separate into two groups, corresponding to FSS and CS, highlighting differences between these conditions.

sec.title: Taxonomic analysis of samples
sec.p:
We performed a taxonomic classification of all amplicon sequence variants (ASVs) identified in this study; Fig. 4 presents the bacterial community composition at the family level across the four sample categories, represented as stacked bar charts. Differences in relative abundance patterns were observed between feces and tissue samples. Fecal samples from CS and FSS were mainly dominated by Lachnospiraceae, Ruminococcaceae, Oscillospiraceae, and Bacteroidaceae, with additional contributions from Tannerellaceae, Akkermansiaceae, Muribaculaceae, Bifidobacteriaceae, Acidaminococcaceae, Burkholderiaceae_A, and Enterobacteriaceae_A. While the same major families were present in both CS and FSS, their relative abundances varied among individual samples. On the other hand, tissue samples (JCP and SCT) displayed a different proportional distribution compared to fecal samples. In JCP, Enterobacteriaceae_A and Fusobacteriaceae showed higher relative abundance in several samples, together with variable contributions from Lachnospiraceae, Ruminococcaceae, and Bacteroidaceae. SCT samples shared many of the same families observed in JCP, including Lachnospiraceae, Ruminococcaceae, Oscillospiraceae, and Bacteroidaceae, although their proportional representation differed across paired specimens.Fig. 4
Family-level microbial composition in fecal and tissue samples. Stacked bar plots showing the relative abundance of the most prevalent bacterial families across sample groups. (A) Fecal samples from healthy controls (CS) and food-sensitized children with juvenile colorectal polyps (FSS). (B) Tissue samples including juvenile colorectal polyps (JCP) and surrounding control tissues (SCT). (C) Taxonomic annotation of the families represented in the stacked bars. Only the most abundant families are displayed; remaining taxa are grouped as “Others.” Each bar represents one individual sample, and relative abundances are expressed as proportions of total reads per sample.

Subsequent analyses focused on identifying bacterial genera and species showing significant differences in relative abundance across the groups. The comparison of relative bacterial abundance at the genus level revealed significant differences between FSS and CS samples (Fig. 5). Using ANCOM-BC for compositional differential abundance analysis, we identified multiple genera that were significantly altered in fecal samples from FSS patients compared to CS. Several taxa were significantly enriched in FSS, including Prevotella, Phascolarctobacterium_A_39470, Sutterella, Catenibacterium, Coprococcus_A_121497, Allisonella, Limosilactobacillus, Senegalimassilia, among others. Conversely, genera such as Akkermansia, UBA5905, Parasutterella_564865, Phascolarctobacterium_A_40086, Veillonella_A, Intestinimonas, Eubacterium_R, Gemmiger_A_73276, Negativibacillus, in addition to other significantly altered taxa were significantly reduced in FSS relative to CS.Fig. 5
Taxonomically annotated ASV (Amplicon Sequence Variants) with significant differential abundance between the FSS (n = 11) and CS (n = 22) groups. Results are based on ANCOM-BC analysis. Bar lengths represent the logarithmic change in estimated absolute abundance relative to CS. Red bars indicate enriched taxa in the FSS group, while blue bars indicate decreased taxa. Taxon labels correspond to the genus level (prefix g__). ASVs without genus label were excluded from the plot but are listed in Table S1 (in all cases q < 0.05 after FDR correction).

Species-level ANCOM-BC analysis further refined the compositional differences observed between FSS and CS (Supplementary Fig. 2). Among the species significantly enriched in FSS, Segatella copri displayed the highest positive fold-change, followed by Collinsella sp000434535, Sutterella wadsworthensis, Phascolarctobacterium A39470 succinatutens, Dorea longicatena, and Prevotella stercorea. Conversely, FSS samples showed a marked depletion of several species compared to CS, most prominently Phocaeicola vulgatus, Dysosmobacter welbionis, Akkermansia muciniphila, Eubacterium sp003491505, Ruminococcus bromii, and Alistipes finegoldii.

Genus-level ANCOM-BC analysis revealed distinct microbial profiles across comparisons (Fig. 6). In the JCP versus CS analysis, JCP samples showed significant enrichment of genera such as Escherichia, Fusobacterium_A, Streptococcus, and Acinetobacter, whereas taxa including Vescimonas and Roseburia were reduced.Fig. 6
Differential abundance analysis of the microbiota associated with JCP. Differentially abundant taxa at the genus (g_) level of JCP against CS (A), JCP against FSS (B), and JCP against SCT groups (C). Bar lengths represent the logarithmic change in estimated absolute abundance relative to CS, FSS, and SCT, respectively. Red bars indicate enriched taxa in the FSS group, while blue bars indicate decreased taxa. Taxon labels correspond to the genus level (prefix g__). ASVs without a genus label were excluded from the plot but are listed in Table S1 (in all cases with q < 0.05 after FDR correction). Number of samples analyzed (n) for CS = 22, FSS = 11, JCP = 14 and SCT n = 5.

In the JCP versus FSS comparison, several genera were significantly increased in JCP, including Escherichia, Akkermansia, and Fusobacterium_A, while Prevotella, Anaerobutyricum, Roseburia_A 166,204, and Angelakisella were decreased relative to FSS. Notably, certain genera that were previously found to be depleted in FSS compared to controls (e.g., Akkermansia) were enriched in JCP when compared to FSS, indicating differential abundance patterns in tissue versus feces samples.

Similarly, in the JCP versus SCT comparison, JCP exhibited higher levels of genera such as Blautia_A_141781, Phocaeicola_A, Dorea_A and Fusobacterium A, whereas Sphingomonas L 486,704 and Sutterella, were reduced relative to SCT.

At species level, ANCOM-BC analysis further refined the genus-level differences observed across comparisons (Supplementary Fig. 3). In the JCP versus CS comparison (panel A), JCP samples were enriched in species such as Bacteroides fragilis, Akkermansia muciniphila, and Parabacteroides distasonis, while several taxa including Fusicatenibacter saccarivorans and Vescimonas sp were reduced.

In the JCP versus FSS analysis (panel B), species including Bacteroides fragilis, Parabacteroides distasonis, and Akkermansia muciniphila, and were significantly increased in JCP, whereas Segatella copri, Roseburia inulinivorans, and Anaerobutyricum hallii were decreased relative to FSS. Similarly, in the JCP versus SCT comparison (panel C), JCP samples exhibited higher abundance of species such as Parabacteroides distasonis, Blautia A 741,781 fusiformis and Dorea A longicatena, while taxa including Sutterella wadsworthensis and Lentihominibacter butyrica showed reduced levels compared to SCT.
Complete microbial profiles for the CS, FSS, JCP and SCT groups and their comparisons are provided in Supplementary Tables 2 (at genus level) and 3 (at species level).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: In this pilot study, we provide an initial characterization of the microbiota associated with JCP, identifying distinctive microbial signatures in both fecal and polyp tissues that may be linked to allergic inflammation and polyp formation. While these findings offer novel insights, the relatively small sample size—particularly in the FSS and SCT groups—limits statistical power and warrants cautious interpretation, and thus the results should be considered exploratory.

Several studies show that microbial diversity is essential for human health20,21, and that diminished bacterial variability may be related to several diseases including colorectal polyps22,23, colorectal cancer24,25, and allergy26,27. In our study, although α-diversity did not differ significantly among feces from FSS, CS, polyp tissues, or surrounding biopsies, β-diversity analyses clearly distinguished fecal from tissue samples and FSS from CS. These results suggest that compositional differences, rather than overall richness or evenness, are key features distinguishing these groups. These observations are consistent with previous studies showing that allergic status and tissue microenvironments can shape microbial community composition28,29. Importantly, as fecal and tissue samples were obtained from independent cohorts rather than paired individuals, comparisons between these compartments reflect between-group patterns rather than within-subject ecological differences and should be interpreted with caution. In addition, the use of different DNA extraction kits and processing workflows for fecal and tissue samples represents a potential source of batch effects, which may contribute to the observed differences between sample types. Therefore, interpretations regarding stool versus tissue differences should be made carefully.

The differential abundance analysis performed by ANCOM-BC revealed a distinct microbial signature in fecal samples from FSS compared to healthy controls. Among the taxa enriched in FSS, Prevotella and Sutterella have been previously associated with mucosal immune modulation and inflammatory conditions. Although several studies suggest Prevotella as protective for allergy30,31, others reported its link to cows’ milk32 and in wheat allergies33. Prevotella spp. have also been related to several pathological intestinal conditions such as ulcerative colitis34 and colorectal cancer35. This apparent dual role may depend on the microbiota context, host immune status, and other environmental factors. Under certain conditions Prevotella may act as a pathobiont, thus contributing to inflammation and pathogenesis through the production of several virulence factors36. Sutterella has been reported in association with immune-mediated and gastrointestinal disorders in pediatric populations, and recently Sutterella-SP-6FBBBH3 has been included in a panel of five bacteria from the nasal cavity that may predict allergic rhinitis37. Although these bacterias’ precise functional role remains context-dependent, their expansion may reflect shifts in host–microbe interactions in sensitized children. Higher levels of Allisonella were also found in FSS compared to CS samples. This bacterium is capable of decarboxylating histidine to produce histamine38, a mediator involved in allergic responses39. Allisonella has been associated with skin conditions such as acne and with intestinal inflammatory disorders40,41. Enterocytes have H2R receptors for histamine, along with immune cells from the mucosae, including eosinophils and mast cells, which may be relevant in a context of increased barrier permeability. Increased histamine levels in the gastrointestinal tract have been associated with the development of food allergies, and other gastrointestinal diseases such as allergic enteropathy and inflammatory bowel disease42.

Conversely, several genera reduced in FSS are commonly associated with intestinal homeostasis. Notably, Akkermansia, a mucin-degrading bacterium linked to epithelial barrier integrity and metabolic health, was significantly decreased43. Low Akkermansia levels in neonates have been linked to atopy and asthma development, and Akkermansia muciniphila has been proposed as a next generation probiotic for inflammatory gut diseases and allergies44. In addition, reductions in genera such as Intestinimonas, Eubacterium, and Gemmiger—taxa frequently associated with short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) production—suggest a potential decrease in microbial functions related to butyrate generation and epithelial support45–47. SCFAs are known to contribute to regulatory immune responses and intestinal barrier stability, and their reduction has been associated with allergic and inflammatory conditions48,49. Interestingly, some of the depleted genera in FSS, including Akkermansia and several butyrate-producing taxa, have also been reported as reduced in inflammatory bowel disease and colorectal cancer, although JCP are hamartomatous benign lesions43,50,51, and histologic abnormalities are low. These parallels likely reflect shared inflammatory ecological patterns.

At the tissue level, JCP samples exhibited a microbial profile distinct from fecal communities. Across comparisons, JCP were enriched in genera such as Escherichia, Fusobacterium, Streptococcus and, Acinetobacter. These taxa include facultative anaerobes frequently reported in association with mucosal inflammation and epithelial stress52–54. Their enrichment may reflect local environmental changes within the polyp niche, such as altered oxygen availability, mucus structure, or immune activation.

In contrast, genera reduced in JCP relative to controls—including Roseburia and Anaerobutyricum—are commonly associated with butyrate production and anaerobic fermentation54. The decreased representation of these taxa suggests a localized shift in metabolic potential within polyp tissue. Importantly, the enrichment of Akkermansia in JCP relative to FSS feces underscores the ecological divergence between luminal and mucosa-associated microbiota, indicating that stool profiles do not necessarily recapitulate tissue-level alterations. We speculate that increased tissue-associated Akkermansia may be associated with alterations in the mucus layer, potentially facilitating the access of other bacteria to the mucosa.

Comparison between JCP and SCT revealed partial taxonomic overlap but quantitative differences, including higher levels of Blautia, Phocaeicola, Dorea, and Fusobacterium in JCP. These findings suggest that polyps are characterized not by the presence of entirely unique microbial taxa, but by localized restructuring of resident communities. The enrichment of Dorea and Phocaeicola is noteworthy, as species within these genera have been associated with mucosal inflammation and barrier alterations in other contexts55,56. Although typically considered gut commensals, their expansion in polyp tissue may reflect adaptation to a locally altered microenvironment and is consistent with a potential context-dependent shift in host–microbe interactions.

Overall, our results suggest that food-sensitized children with JCP exhibit a dual microbial pattern: fecal communities marked by reduced representation of barrier-supporting and SCFA-associated taxa, and polyp tissues enriched in genera previously associated with inflammatory microenvironments. Rather than indicating overt neoplastic processes, these patterns may reflect interactions between allergic-type immune activation and local mucosal remodeling.

From a clinical perspective, the presence of genera previously associated with inflammatory or neoplasia-related contexts within benign polyps warrants careful longitudinal investigation. However, given the cross-sectional design and the benign nature of JCP, causal relationships cannot be inferred. Additional limitations of our study include the absence of extraction blanks during library construction, which represents a significant limitation, particularly for low-biomass tissue samples, where contamination may substantially influence the observed microbial profiles. Although we implemented a stringent filtering strategy to exclude likely contaminant samples, this approach does not fully substitute for the inclusion of proper negative controls and therefore low-biomass results should be interpreted with particular caution. Additional limitations include the use of two different DNA extraction kits for feces and tissue samples, which may introduce bias, the relatively small sample size, and the lack of paired fecal and tissue samples from the same individuals, which precluded direct within-subject compartmental comparisons. Although ANCOM-BC improves statistical robustness in small cohorts, the differential abundance results should be interpreted as exploratory and require validation in larger populations. Furthermore, serological testing was not performed in CS patients, as blood sampling was not ethically justified in asymptomatic children. Allergy status in this group was determined through structured clinical questionnaires, which may limit the precision of classification, thus, the possibility of undetected sensitization in this group cannot be excluded. Potential confounders such as environmental exposures or early-life factors, were not systematically recorded and therefore could not be formally analyzed.

Future studies integrating longitudinal sampling, functional metagenomics, and host immune profiling will be necessary to determine whether the observed microbial shifts contribute to polyp biology or represent secondary responses to tissue-level alterations. Larger cohorts and mechanistic approaches (e.g., gnotobiotic models and metabolomics) will be essential to clarify whether these microbial patterns are involved in polyp initiation, maintenance, or progression, and to better understand the links between specific taxa, type 2 inflammation, and food antigen sensitization.

sec.title: Patient enrolment and sample collection
sec.p: Pediatric patients were assisted at the Gastroenterology Unit at the Children’s Hospital in La Plata for painless rectal bleeding. All patients included in the protocol were indicated a colonoscopy for surveillance of polyps. In all cases, polyps were removed (n = 23). Biopsies from polyps’ adjacent tissue were also obtained for analysis (n = 8).

All patients were further evaluated at the Allergy Unit. Food sensitization was assessed by skin prick tests and serum IgE determination. Total and food-specific IgE levels were measured as previously described by Docena et al.57. Samples corresponding to one polyp (JCP15) were excluded from further analyses due to negative results for both total and food-specific IgE.

Due to the low microbial biomass inherent in intestinal polyp tissue, a stringent quality control pipeline to distinguish true biological signals from potential contamination of tissue samples was implemented. A reference set of expected intestinal taxa consisting of 86 genera previously identified in the Human Gut Microbiome Atlas (Human Gut Microbiome Atlas available from https://www.microbiomeatlas.org) was defined. For each sample, we calculated two diagnostic parameters: the cumulative relative abundance of these 86 reference genera and the Shannon diversity index (entropy). A bivariate analysis (raster plot in Supplementary Fig. 4) revealed a clear bimodal distribution of samples. One group exhibited high concordance with the reference atlas and balanced diversity, while a second group of nine samples was identified as outliers due to extremely low percentage of known intestinal taxa and a low Shannon entropy. These outlier samples were dominated by non-intestinal, opportunistic genera; specifically, samples SCT8, JCP18, and JCP17, for example, present Pseudomonas (> 40%) and Halomonas (> 10%), which are common hospital-associated contaminants. To ensure the integrity of the results, these nine samples were excluded from all subsequent analyses, and from Table 1, thus rendering 14 reliable samples of JCP and 5 of SCT. This filtering approach ensured that the reported microbiome profiles represent the endogenous tissue-associated community rather than exogenous noise.Table 1

Fecal samples were collected at home using occult fecal blood collection cards (HEM-CHECK-1, Veda Lab, France). Eleven stool samples from food-sensitized children with colorectal polyps (FSS) and twenty-two from healthy children without allergic or infectious diseases (CS) were included. Fecal samples were collected prior to bowel preparation for colonoscopy (when applicable), thus minimizing potential microbiota alterations associated with cleansing procedures. Patients were excluded if they had received systemic or topical antibiotics within the previous four weeks, or had a history of prolonged or chronic antibiotic therapy, or had documented parasitic infections or autoimmune diseases. The absence of allergic disease was assessed through a structured clinical questionnaire administered to the patients and/or their parents, specifically addressing previous diagnoses of allergy and the presence of allergic manifestations (e.g., food-related symptoms, atopic dermatitis, asthma, or rhinitis). The questionnaire included dietary habits. All patients were following common non-restricted diets. Measurement of serum IgE levels was not performed in control subjects for ethical reasons, as these children did not present clinical indications warranting blood extraction solely for research purposes, so we cannot exclude sensitization in the control group.

Fecal samples were collected during an initial recruitment phase, whereas tissue samples were incorporated subsequently as part of an independent cohort. Accordingly, comparisons involving fecal and tissue microbiota represent analyses across distinct participant groups rather than within-subject compartmental assessments.

Parents or legal guardians completed a written questionnaire regarding health and dietary habits before sampling and provided informed consent. The study protocol was approved by the Central Ethics Committee of the Universidad Nacional de La Plata (009-009-21) and by the Institutional Protocol Review Committee of the Sor María Ludovica Children’s Hospital (389-2018, 389-2023). Demographic information regarding patients analyzed in this study is depicted in Table 1. All experiments were performed in accordance with relevant guidelines and regulations.

sec.title: Genomic DNA extraction from tissue and fecal samples
sec.p: DNA extraction was performed from 200 mg of feces using QIAamp PowerFecal DNA Kit (Qiagen, Tecnolab, Argentina), according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Tissue samples (200 mg) were minced using an Ultra-turrax T25 homogenizer (IKA Brazil, Brazil), and DNA was extracted using the TIANamp Stool DNA Kit (TianGen Biotech, Beijing, China) following the manufacturer’s instructions. Nucleic acid integrity, purity, and concentration were evaluated by 0.8% agarose gel electrophoresis and on a Varioskan Lux multimode microplate reader (Thermo Fisher Scientific, MA, USA).

sec.title: 16S rRNA gene amplification
sec.p: The V3-V4 region of the 16S rRNA gene was amplified from fecal and tissue samples using the universal bacterial and archaeal primers Bakt_341F/Bakt_805R (Macrogen, Seoul, South Korea). Sequencing was performed using the Illumina MiSeq platform (Macrogen, Seoul, South Korea) with specific adapters. The libraries were sequenced in paired-end mode, and the raw reads have been deposited in the sequence reads archive (SRA) at NCBI.

sec.title: Bioinformatic and statistical analyses
sec.p: The resulting sequence reads were demultiplexed with QIIME2 version 21.4 (https://qiime2.org) by using the Demux plugin58,59. To remove short reads, chimeric sequence reads, singletons and merges paired-end reads, we used the QIIME2 plugin Divisive Amplicon Denoising Algorithm (DADA2)60 with a truncation length of 250 bp. This step results in high-resolution ASV or features for downstream analysis. The resulting quality-filtered feature table of sequence variants was visually inspected to select the sampling depth parameter for sample rarefaction in order to perform the microbial diversity analysis. The α- and β-diversity analysis was performed by using the diversity plugin in QIIME2, to this end we used a sampling depth of 3300, which allowed the inclusion of 11 stool samples from food allergen-sensitized children, 19 stool samples from healthy controls, and 11 polyp samples in the diversity analysis. Alpha-diversity was measured with the Shannon diversity index (SDI)61, and Faith’s phylogenetic diversity62. To determine whether alpha-diversity measures are statistically significant among groups/categories we used the diversity α-group-significance command, which implements the pairwise Kruskal–Wallis test. Additionally, β-diversity was measured using the weighted and unweighted Unique Fraction (UniFrac) metric. To determine whether UniFrac distances among samples within a category are statistically significant, we used the QIIME diversity β-group-significance command to run a permutational multivariate analysis of variance (PERMANOVA)63. β-Diversity was visualized by principal coordinate analysis (PCoA) using the Emperor plugin64 through QIIME2.

Taxonomic annotation of features obtained from all samples listed in Table 1 was also performed in QIIME2 using the naive Bayes strategy with the feature-classifier plugin65. The reference sequences correspond to the Greengenes2 v2024.09 full-length sequences (file: 2024.09.backbone.full-length.nb.qza)66. The resulting absolute abundance tables of annotated features for each sample were exported by means of feature-table tools in QIIME2. To identify differentially abundant taxa among groups, we employed the ANCOM-BC (Analysis of Compositions of Microbiomes with Bias Correction) algorithm67. Unlike traditional non-parametric tests, ANCOM-BC operates on absolute abundance and introduces a sample-specific offset term to account for differences in sampling fractions (sequencing depth) and compositional bias. The model was used to estimate log-fold changes (LFC) for each taxon. P-values were adjusted for multiple comparisons using the Benjamini-Hochberg (FDR) procedure, with significance defined at a q-value < 0.05. Results are compiled in Supplementary Tables 2 and 3.

notes.title: Data availability
notes.p: The datasets generated and analyzed during the current study are available in the NCBI Sequence Read Archive (SRA) under BioProject accession number PRJNA1364002. Comparison and statistical data are provided in Supplementary Tables 2 and 3. Sample metadata, including patient characteristics and experimental variables used for microbiome analyses, are provided in Supplementary Table 4. Embedded hyperlinks direct to the corresponding entries in the NCBI BioSample database, with links to associated Sequence Read Archive (SRA) records, providing access to raw sequencing data.
